title: El Niño Is Driving a Record Marine Heat Wave Off the California Coast
gist: A developing super El Niño, likely the strongest on record, is stacking on top of a marine heat wave that has persisted since January 2025 and on long-term warming, producing record subsurface ocean temperatures and steric sea-level heights off California. Scripps glider data and climate scientists tie the heat to Kelvin waves, coastal flooding, 30-foot waves, record hourly rainfall and rare waterspouts over San Francisco Bay.

insights.claim: Scripps oceanographer Daniel Rudnick's underwater glider data show subsurface temperature anomalies off California so extreme that the color scale of his anomaly chart had to be readjusted, and heat-driven (steric) sea-level height is at the highest level he has seen in 20 years of collection.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Heat stored hundreds of meters deep means the anomaly is unlikely to dissipate quickly, extending weather and fisheries impacts along the California coast.
insights.quote: I looked back at our data to make sure that I'm not making a mistake and it's correct—and it is,
insights.locator: A color-coded chart showing temperature anomalies

insights.claim: In late October a Monterey Bay station recorded a record 64.72°F (18.18°C) at 200 feet depth, while San Diego data showed 77°F at the same depth, an anomaly of 21.3°F above normal.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Anomalies of this size at depth are a stress signal for marine ecosystems and coastal fisheries and a leading indicator for storm intensity.

themes.theme: Stacked drivers: El Niño on warming baseline

insights.claim: The 2026 El Niño is shaping up to be the strongest on record, exceeding the 2015–2016 super El Niño, and Rudnick calls El Niño the biggest source of climate variability off the California coast.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A record El Niño has global knock-on effects on weather, agriculture and energy demand that investors should track beyond California.
insights.quote: It’s fair to say it’s off the charts,
insights.locator: El Niño “is the biggest source of climate variability”

insights.claim: The unprecedented California ocean conditions result from three stacked factors: a strong El Niño, a coastal marine heat wave running since January 2025 (up to 8°F above average in August), and human-caused warming of about 1.8°F off Southern California since the 1970s.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A higher warming baseline means each future El Niño is more likely to produce record extremes, raising the frequency of tail events for coastal insurers and utilities.
insights.quote: The heat we get from El Niño stacking on top of the heat we already have, that’s the thing that makes this most unusual,
insights.locator: This year’s El Niño is adding heat

insights.claim: Kelvin waves carry warm water west to east across the Pacific and push down the thermocline, which warms the ocean by suppressing cooling rather than adding a deep heat source, and also raise California sea levels by keeping water from moving offshore.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
entities: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
insights.so_what: Understanding the Kelvin-wave mechanism helps anticipate how long elevated coastal sea levels and warmth will persist during El Niño events.
insights.quote: It isn't like there's some heater in the deep ocean suddenly,
insights.locator: Part of what’s driving the higher ocean temperatures

insights.claim: Higher sea levels from Kelvin waves and thermal expansion have amplified weeks of California coastal flooding, with waves over 30 feet that set off seismographs and hourly rainfall records set from San Francisco to Burbank.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Watch for flood-related insured losses, infrastructure damage and utility disruption in coastal California through the rainy season.
insights.locator: Californians have been living through several weeks

insights.claim: Rare twin waterspouts formed over San Francisco Bay when cold storm air moved over unusually warm water, a phenomenon normally associated with Florida or the Mediterranean rather than the usually frigid Pacific.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Novel weather phenomena in a region signal that historical risk models for California coastal weather may understate current hazards.
insights.quote: The air temperatures are somewhat winter-like right now, but the water ain't,
insights.locator: The warm water is driving weather
